candidates.headline: Fine-grained QoS classes do not guarantee fairness across request lengths.
candidates.claim: Defining interactive and non-interactive QoS classes with per-request deadlines does not ensure fair SLO attainment across short and long requests; fairness depends on hybrid prioritization, alpha, and relegation.
candidates.paper_fact: As 𝛼 increases, the system increasingly deprioritizes longer requests. This significantly reduces median latency for all requests but comes at the cost of violating deadlines for most long requests.
candidates.premise: QoS classes encode latency targets, not a fairness policy; scheduling priority and overload handling determine which requests actually meet those targets.
candidates.inference: Because QoServe's priority formula includes an alpha-weighted remaining-work term and relegation can drop requests, fine-grained classes alone cannot guarantee fair treatment; the paper's own alpha sweep shows a median-vs-long-request tradeoff.
candidates.toy_example: Not a measurement: two requests share a QoS class but have different remaining prefill lengths; with a large alpha, the shorter one is scheduled first and the longer one may miss its deadline.
candidates.conditional_consequence: Under overload or aggressive alpha tuning, long requests in a class may be deprioritized even though the class's SLO is nominally the same.
candidates.critical_link: The link is that QoS class -> deadline does not specify a tie-break or fairness rule; the scheduler's alpha and relegation policy fill that gap and can shift violations toward long requests.

candidates.headline: Available deadline slack does not guarantee dynamic chunking gains under high load or tight TBT.
candidates.claim: Dynamic chunking's throughput benefit depends on accumulated deadline slack; when load is high or TBT is strict, slack is exhausted and chunk size reverts toward the smaller latency-safe value.
candidates.paper_fact: QoServe benefits from dynamically increasing chunk size by exploiting any deadline slack of the non-interactive QoS requests as well as any slack of interactive requests during lower load.
candidates.premise: Slack is the difference between a request's next-token deadline and current time; high load and strict TBT reduce slack, so chunk-size increases are regime-dependent rather than universal.
candidates.inference: An artifact run at high load or with tight TBT may show smaller dynamic-chunking gains than the paper's 20% result, and those gains should not be generalized to all load regimes.
candidates.toy_example: Toy example (not a measurement): with 50 ms TBT and little slack, a larger chunk may consume the budget; with large accumulated slack, the same policy can grow the chunk safely.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If the artifact evaluates dynamic chunking under high load or strict TBT, then expect smaller chunks and lower chunking benefit; do not infer a mechanism failure from load-dependent gains alone.
candidates.critical_link: The critical link is slack availability: the mechanism converts deadline slack into larger prefill chunks, so without slack there is no safe room to increase chunk size.

non-interactive TTLT dominates and slack remains

do_not_infer: Do not infer that dynamic chunking always improves throughput; the authors scope slack exploitation to available slack and lower load.

candidates.headline: Conservative underprediction of chunk size does not guarantee end-to-end QoS safety.
candidates.claim: Tuning the predictor to under-predict chunk size reduces over-prediction risk and throughput, but it does not by itself guarantee that all requests meet TTFT/TBT/TTLT deadlines under prediction error, queueing, or profile drift.
candidates.paper_fact: We tune the model to err on the side of under-predicting chunk size.
candidates.premise: A conservative bias in one control variable can reduce one failure mode while leaving other latency sources (decode queue, scheduling, prefill backlog, model error) able to violate deadlines; safety requires the bias to dominate all relevant errors.
candidates.inference: The paper reports a deliberate underprediction bias and says it avoids inadvertent latency increase from over-prediction. That supports a risk-reduction claim, not a guarantee of QoS; the guarantee would require bounded residual error and deadline enforcement beyond the quoted design choice.
candidates.toy_example: Toy example (not a measurement): if the predictor under-predicts chunk size by 10% but the decode queue adds a large delay, the batch can still miss its TBT deadline despite the conservative chunk choice.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If underprediction margin exceeds execution-time error and the scheduler accounts for decode slack and queueing, the bias can protect latency; if not, QoS can still fail.
candidates.critical_link: The bias changes the chosen chunk size, but deadline compliance is determined by actual batch latency plus queueing and decode constraints; the link from bias to QoS is conditional.

candidates.headline: Hybrid prioritization does not imply or guarantee overload SLO attainment; eager relegation is a separate necessary mechanism.
candidates.claim: Hybrid prioritization alone does not guarantee QoS under overload; the paper's overload results depend on eager relegation to prevent cascading deadline violations.
candidates.paper_fact: Our hybrid prioritization strikes a balance between minimizing deadline violations and fairness. However, as shown in Figure 5, under overload conditions, QoServe (or any scheduling policy) still cannot service all incoming requests at the desired QoS SLOs.
candidates.premise: Scheduling heuristics alone cannot create capacity; when demand exceeds service rate, some requests must be dropped, delayed, or relegated.
candidates.inference: Therefore hybrid prioritization is not sufficient by itself for overload SLOs; the paper couples it with eager relegation to maintain service for the majority.
candidates.toy_example: Toy example (not a measurement): if 10 jobs arrive per second and capacity is 8, a priority order alone cannot serve all 10; relegating 2 prevents queue cascade.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If overload exceeds capacity and relegation is disabled or ineffective, hybrid prioritization cannot by itself maintain SLOs for all requests.
candidates.critical_link: The critical link is capacity: hybrid prioritization orders work but does not reduce total work; relegation removes or deprioritizes requests to prevent cascading violations.
